item.title: Why Our Brains Hate High Gas Prices
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Why Our Brains Hate High Gas Prices

We stand and watch the numbers climb and the pain of paying grows.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Paying for gas feels worse than most purchases because we pay while we consume, and watch the cost climb.
  • Drivers search for cheaper gas when prices rise, but once prices fall and the pain eases, they stop looking.
  • Expecting gas prices to rise makes us expect everything else to rise, too.

The national average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. is breaking records. Evidence of the ongoing cost-of-living crisis is everywhere, but nowhere do shoppers feel its impacts more than at the gas station.

You pull in on the way to work. You lift the nozzle and watch the numbers on the pump start to climb. And climb. And keep on climbing, long past the point where you would usually expect them to stop. Meanwhile, the tank is still only half full.

It is not a pleasant experience. Paying for gas can feel far worse than paying for the same amount for almost anything else.

So why does filling up hurt so much?

Pain at the pumps

Generally, by the time we consume something, paying for it has become a distant memory. The two are usually kept at a comfortable distance from one another, so our attention is on what we have bought, usually not on how much we paid for it.

For example, you might buy a coffee to go, leave the store and drink it later once it has cooled to a more palatable temperature. By then, you have forgotten what it cost, or you are too distracted by how nice it tastes to remember. You pay for Netflix once a month, but the payment is automated, so you are even further removed from the purchase as the money leaves your bank account automatically. You don’t think about how much you are paying for the streaming service when watching their latest TV series.

The experience of paying for gas, however, is different. We pay while we consume. The running total is right in front of our eyes as the cents tick by, faster and faster.

Prelec and Loewenstein (1998) called the unpleasant feeling experienced when handing over money the pain of paying. They argued that this pain is at its worst when paying and consuming happen at the same time, because there is no escaping the instant reminder of the costs. Few purchases bundle paying and consuming together quite as tightly as filling up a car.

The numbers tick by faster, and the pain felt increases, too
Source: Erik Mclean (introspectivedsgn) / Pexels

The taxi meter effect

Consumers dislike this feeling so much that they may pay extra to avoid it. Lambrecht and Skiera (2006) studied thousands of customers of an internet provider who could choose between paying for what they used or paying a flat monthly fee. Many chose the flat fee, even when paying only for only what they used would have been cheaper.

The researchers used the taxi meter effect to explain this behaviour. Watching the meter slowly climb from the back seat of a cab can cause discomfort for passengers. People feel pain when they know a meter is running and can see the evidence of it. With a flat fee, however, you never have to watch or worry, so you enjoy exactly the same service more without being reminded constantly of how much it is costing you.

The same happens at the gas pump, only worse. Customers have to stand and watch the numbers get larger, and there is nothing they can do about it.

Going the extra mile

When prices go up, many drivers start shopping around. They may search price comparison apps or be willing to drive a little further across town in their commitment to finding a cheaper price. It may seem rational to shop around, but the money saved by driving further to a cheaper gas station is negligible if it takes more gas to get there.

The way drivers react when gas prices rise is rather different from how they react when prices start to fall. Researchers Lewis and Marvel (2011) tracked visits to a gas price comparison website where drivers report and compare local gas prices. They found that people searched for cheaper gas more when prices were rising than when they were falling.

In the context of the pain of paying, that makes sense. When prices at the pump are climbing, every little saving matters, so drivers go looking for a price closer to what they consider reasonable or what they are used to paying. When prices start to fall, the pain eases, so people stop looking and slip back into their usual habit of buying wherever is most convenient.

Running on empty

The price crisis at the pumps is also changing how people view the wider cost-of-living crisis. Sung and Kim (2026) found that when people expect gas prices to go up, they expect the price of everything else to rise, too. When they expect gas prices to go down, however, their expectations about everything else do not change. They also found that the effect was stronger for households on the lowest incomes than for those on the highest.

Given how fast prices are rising, not just at the pumps but across the marketplace, consumers are having to accept that they will only feel more pain when paying.

item.title: When Knowing Yourself Keeps You Stuck
item.description:
Personality

When Knowing Yourself Keeps You Stuck

How self-awareness can become a ceiling instead of a foundation.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Personality traits describe how you tend to act. They are not instructions for what you have to do next.
  • Self-awareness tends to become a liability when a useful description hardens into an identity to defend.
  • Knowing your personality starting point is the first step toward shifting it, not a reason to stop there.

A client came in recently with a familiar problem. Her manager kept making decisions without consulting her, which was exhausting her. When I suggested we work on some assertiveness skills so she could set a clearer boundary, she thought about it for a second. "I can try," she said. "But I'm just not an assertive person. I'm an INFJ."

I hear some version of this all the time. The introverted, intuitive, feeling, and judging personality label shows up as the explanation, the evidence, and the reason not to bother. And what made it complicated was that she wasn't wrong about herself. She is thoughtful, reserved, and less likely to push back in the moment. But that description was doing more work than she had examined.

What Personality Actually Is

Psychologists who study personality converge on a model called the Big Five, which captures five core dimensions: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (which I prefer to call emotional sensitivity, because it describes a tendency toward strong feelings, not a character flaw).

Think of these five dimensions as sliders on a soundboard. Everyone has their own unique combination of settings. Some people are high on agreeableness and lower on extraversion. Others are high on conscientiousness with moderate emotional sensitivity. The specific mix is your personality profile.

Those sliders describe how you have tended to think, feel, and behave across situations and over time. They are statistical tendencies, not mechanical rules. A trait does not explain why you act the way you do, and it does not control what you do next.

When Self-Knowledge Is an Asset

Knowing your patterns is genuinely useful. If you tend toward introversion, you can structure your week to include recovery time after intensive social demands. If you score higher on emotional sensitivity, you can anticipate when certain situations are likely to hit harder and plan accordingly.

Good self-knowledge helps you work with your tendencies rather than against them. The goal of understanding your personality is not to flatten yourself into a four-letter code. It is to have honest, actionable information about where you are starting from.

When the Label Becomes a Limit

The trouble starts when that description stops being information and becomes a verdict.

Research suggests that people with a more rigid self-concept tend to have a harder time updating their behavior when circumstances call for it. An accurate observation about yourself can harden into a prediction, and the prediction starts functioning like a wall.

My client was not wrong that she tends toward introversion and agreeableness. But "I'm an INFJ" was doing something different in that moment. It was not informing her decision. It was making it for her.

That shift happens quietly. A useful pattern becomes an identity, and we protect identities. What started as self-awareness gradually becomes the reason not to try something new.

How Personality Shifts

Personality traits shift. Not overnight, and not by deciding to be different, but meaningfully, with targeted practice over time. My own clinical research suggests people can see roughly 20 years of natural personality shift in under 20 weeks with skill-based work.

Insight is where that process starts. You cannot begin a change journey without knowing where you are. The problem was not that my client knew she tended to avoid conflict. The problem was that she treated her starting point as her destination.

Knowing your trait profile is the first step. It tells you which sliders are worth moving and where to focus your effort. It does not tell you what is possible, and it certainly does not tell you where to stop.

item.title: How to Live as Long as the Richest, Without the Rat Race
item.description:
Spirituality

How to Live as Long as the Richest, Without the Rat Race

Monastic life seems to level inequalities in longevity.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Wealth shapes both how long we live and how long we live in good health.
  • Shared resources, routine, community, and purpose may help explain the longevity and equality of monks.
  • A life organised around purpose and belonging can be rich without wealth, comparison, or competition.
Harvest at the Abbaye de Lérins, on an island opposite Cannes, c. 1900.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Public domain

Recently, I decided to reach out to a childhood friend. We hadn’t spoken in 25 years.

He wasn’t just any childhood friend. We were born on the same day, in the same town, one hour apart. We used to joke that we were twins from different mothers.

Over the years, he became a Trappist monk: a strict kind of monk who practises deep silence and speaks only when necessary. I write him long, flowing letters; he replies laconically, but touchingly.

His life is austere. Every morning, he wakes up at 3:30 to pray. And yet I find myself envying something in it: its simplicity, its mindfulness, and its constant, if mostly silent, companionship.

My twin brother got me thinking about the monastic life. As I researched, I found something astonishing: If you are poor and uneducated, you may enjoy the same health outcomes and life expectancy as the richest and most educated—simply by becoming a monk or nun.

This remarkable fact ought to be better known, and probably would be if it did not sit so uneasily with our cut-throat consumerist society.

The Price of Inequality

A major American study found that, at age 40, the richest 1 percent of men could expect to live 14.8 years longer than the poorest 1 percent. For women, the gap was 10.6 years.

The inequality is not just in how long people live, but how well. In England, people born in the most deprived areas in 2018-20 could expect nearly 20 fewer years in good health than those born in the least deprived areas: 19.3 fewer years for women, and 18.6 for men.

In a monastery, these inequalities vanish. A 2025 study followed 2,421 German Catholic monks born between 1840 and 1959. The researchers used the order’s titles “brother” and “padre” as indicators of socioeconomic status, with brothers often engaged in manual labour and the better-educated padres holding senior administrative posts. Across the different birth cohorts, they found no statistically significant survival difference between the two groups.

The contrast is all the more striking because monks appear not only to escape the inequality between rich and poor, but also to live unusually long lives. A study of Bavarian religious communities found that young adult monks could expect to live up to four years longer than other men. A Korean study analysing newspaper death notices across occupational groups between 1963 and 2010 found that clergy, including Buddhist monks, had the highest reported average age at death, at about 80.

Cloistered life reduces inequality not just between rich and poor, but also between men and women. A girl born in America in 2024 could expect to live 4.9 years longer than her male counterpart. By contrast, a study of Bavarian religious communities found that nuns' life expectancy exceeded monks’ by only about one year.

A Different Way to Live

What might explain this all-round levelling effect? In a monastery, many of the things that make life better and safer are shared. Monks eat together, live under the same roof, follow a common routine, and receive the same care.

The monastery also offers something harder to measure: a place within a community, useful work, and a strong sense of purpose. Its members have a role and a status, but little of the competition that governs life outside. They have peace without being alone. Even death belongs to a shared—and continuing—story.

The implication that you can “win at life” by stepping out of the rat race is, of course, deeply disturbing. Our society assumes that income and education represent genuine advantages. But the monastery suggests that they matter partly because the world outside is insecure, competitive, and unequal. Once people share the same housing, food, healthcare, community, and purpose, much of the advantage of wealth and education disappears.

I think of my friend waking up at 3:30 to pray and chant. His life is austere, but far from empty. Perhaps that is what I envy: not the silence alone, but the sense that a life can be rich—in fact, far richer—without being organised around acquisition, comparison, and the fear of falling behind.

item.title: Prevent Stalking by Recognizing Precursor Behavior
item.description:
Limerence

Prevent Stalking by Recognizing Precursor Behavior

Detecting the longing of limerence: unrequited obsession and fixation.

Posted October 11, 2026

Key points
  • Limerence involves fixation and obsession, which are stalking-type behaviors.
  • Fixation can evolve into obsessive rumination driven by a combination of doubt and hope.
  • Limerence may be a precursor, but does not always evolve into stalking.
Source: Image by Gerd Altmann from Pixabay

Having prosecuted stalkers for 30 years, I am familiar with the recognizable evolution of problematic perpetrator behavior. Some stalkers are motivated by job-related conflict or neighborhood disputes, while others are overcome with feelings of lust, longing, or unrequited love. In all cases, the best plan is not prediction, but prevention. The first step is spotting the red flags.

Uncovering Hidden Obsession

Paula Bradbury et al. (2025) investigated limerence as a precursor to stalking in a piece entitled “Limerence, Hidden Obsession, Fixation, and Rumination.”[i] She defines limerence as an “obsessive attachment” to another individual coupled with an overwhelming longing for his or her attention. She notes this state of unrequited and intense emotion involves fixation and obsession, which are stalking-type behaviors, and recognize that limerence-fueled behavior can progress to harmful external conduct that can develop into stalking.

Bradbury et al. describe limerence as very different from being “in love” or experiencing a crush, because in those emotional states, strong feelings tend to come and go. With limerence, intense longing may continue for years, become an addiction, and potentially evolve into obsessive rumination driven by a combination of doubt and hope. In fact, they note that a higher level of uncertainty as to whether the target returns the affection increases the degree of limerence and rumination, as well as the desire for reciprocation.

Without reciprocation, they recognize that a limerent individual can become consumed by their obsession and resort to imagined reciprocation to sustain their emotional needs. They note that limerence may not only progress into stalking, but it is also devastating to the person suffering from obsessive thoughts, who may experience symptoms including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, self-harm, and disruption of existing relationships.

The Ease of Online Obsession

Limerent individuals can view the targets of their obsession from the comfort of their own homes. This passive monitoring flies under the radar, as Bradbury et al. note that due to the one-sided nature of their obsession, many limerent individuals have fueled their passion in a “highly clandestine manner” for a long period of time.

In seeking to identify factors that escalate or inhibit the progression of obsessive limerent behavior beyond rumination, Bradbury et al. identify accelerants, or enabling factors, as including pervasive use of social media and digital devices, as well as issues related to self-regulation and attachment. They recognize that the internet allows limerent individuals to develop parasocial bonds, sustain maladaptive fantasies, and permit the development of their own narrative, without any contact with the object of their obsession. In fact, they note that observing others on the internet without their consent or knowledge has become normalized, providing a business model of operation for popular social media platforms ranging from TikTok and Instagram to Facebook, to professional networks such as LinkedIn.

Promoting Prevention

The goal is to detect maladaptive feelings before they progress into stalking behavior, which Bradbury et al. suggest is possible by remaining attuned to the conduct of individuals seeking help for obsessive, intrusive thoughts. Noting the strong correlations between limerence and stalking pathways, they argue that the same type of fixated, unrequited, obsessive, and uncertain aspects of stalking behaviors are reflected in the nature of limerence—although with limerence, the traits have not developed into actions that cause fear in the person who is the target of obsession.

Bradbury et al. recognize that although limerence may be a risk factor in some cases, it is not always a stalking precursor. They emphasize the importance of identifying psychological traits that inhibit stalking behavior and promote positive self-regulation, influencing motivation as well as the ability to control actions and behavior. When limerence is operating as a precursor to stalking, Bradbury et al. note that passive actions or behavior may present an opportunity for proactive intervention. And for anyone within the throes of this type of obsessive, intrusive, involuntary state of emotion who is suffering in silence, professional help is available.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
